newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian road row takes toll on government unity.
newsitem.headline: Austrian road row takes toll on government unity.

text.p: Austria's coalition government of Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party faced a rift on Friday over the planned introduction of an electronic road-pricing system for trucks.

The Social Democrats, the senior coalition partner, want to install the pay-per-use system for heavy goods vehicles on motorways straight away so that car drivers do not have to pay for road damage inflicted mainly by trucks.
The conservatives insist Austria should wait for a European Union agreement on the issue.

"We want to bring in a road-pricing system at the same time as the European Union countries so that we don't have the disadvantages of going it alone," conservative Economy Minister Johann Farnleitner told a news conference.
"If we brought a system in on our own the net revenue would ultimately be swallowed by the cost," he said, adding that it would place a heavy burden on the economy.
The row erupted after the publication this week of a report into the feasibility of the project commissioned by the People's Party.
The study puts forward four options for a road-pricing system, with the aim of shifting the financial burden of road maintenance on to heavy goods vehicles.
"The report showed an electronic toll for trucks was technically feasible and economically sensible," Social Democrat Transport Minister Caspar Einem told state radio.
But Farnleitner says it would take at least two years to equip Austria's motorways with the necessary technology. Moreover, a scheme for trucks would inevitably have to involve cars too, he said.
The Social Democrats accused the conservatives of dragging their feet over the issue.
"The conservatives are making out that road-pricing will affect ordinary cars, but that is not under discussion at present," Social Democrat chief whip Peter Kostelka said.
Road-pricing has been a bone of contention recently in Austria which prides itself on high environmental standards.

In January this year Austria introduced an unpopular levy for motorways, charging cars and lorries of up to 3.5 tonnes a flat fee of 550 schillings ($46). Heavy goods vehicles pay more according to their weight.
Many experts maintain the system is unfair to ordinary drivers, many of whom are infrequent users of motorways.
Traffic on Austria's motorways has substantially increased over the past five years, in part through the sudden influx of commercial vehicles from eastern Europe.

Austria also faces a legal battle with the European Commission over an alleged breach of EU legislation after it raised tolls for the use of the Alpine Brenner pass in a bid to reduce traffic on the busy route.
